channel.title: Joseph Noblett: writing
channel.description: Joseph Noblett writes about learning EECS.

item.title: How Will It Feel When I Reach It?
item.description:
I started this EECS program not too long ago. But I’ve been thinking about the day I get a SWE job or finish the program. How will that feel?

The past few years, it’s felt like I’ve been coasting through life. I always felt a draw to software programming, but I could never follow through. Then I realized I hadn’t completed or accomplished anything. I’ve never finished anything I’ve started, and that eats at me. Will that feeling get better as I move through the course? But I want to focus on this: how will it feel when I reach it?

First, I think it will only increase my sense of purpose. Right now it feels like I have gas in the tank I’m not using. But it turns out I am using it. I’m using that fuel to haunt my own thoughts. If I don’t use that fuel, my mind will: by beating myself up, comparing myself to peers, or just bingeing the fuel away. What happens if I use all my fuel? Will I be happy with myself? Will those bad habits still have fuel to run on? If my fuel goes to my purpose, then my purpose will refill my fuel.

Ultimately, I started this because I felt “dumb.” I didn’t have great hearing growing up, so I was in speech therapy until 8th grade. I could barely talk, because I couldn’t hear until I was 6. I had a super hard time sounding out words, because I couldn’t even make the same sounds as everyone else. So, honestly, I never really learned how to spell. And because I couldn’t spell, I drifted away from English classes, which pushed me even further behind. But I believe that once I get these skills, I’ll only get better. I’ll be more confident in my English and writing, which will make me want to write more, and that’s the goal.

Lastly, from all that, you can probably guess that I feel useless right now. I’ve been hard-stuck in fast food for 3 years, in my late 20s, and it sucks. I’m in my “prime.” And since it’s 2026 and AI is advancing like crazy, feeling useless == feeling replaceable by AI. Nobody wants to feel like they can’t contribute to society.

Looking at how I’ve felt in the past, I think, shows me how I’ll feel after completing something like this. I really feel the purpose part. I want to drive toward something bigger. I really believe any human has the capacity to do anything in life. Then I’ll never have to feel dumb or useless again. I’ll know what I studied and how hard I worked to reach this goal. Shoot, I already feel proud of the little progress I’ve made so far. I’m doing it. I’m going to reach it. I’m finally going to complete something!

item.title: Why Your Computer Has Walls Inside It
item.description:
Have you ever wondered why computers have root users and admins? I have. Why is this system needed? Why does a computer hide its complex details from the user? It turns out the same idea runs through almost every complex system today. First I’ll describe the two “spaces” on your Linux machine, then I’ll explain why they’re kept separate.

Two spaces

There are two main areas inside a Linux machine. Kernel space is the orchestration space for the whole operating system. The kernel can read, write, update and delete anything, and it’s the only part that talks to the hardware directly. It acts as the interface between programs and the hardware.

User space is everything you control: folders, processes, GUIs and programs. It’s the interface you use to talk to the kernel, which in turn talks to the hardware (memory and CPU).

Walls for safety

Having two spaces limits what a user can touch. You can’t accidentally crash the whole system by typing the wrong command, because your programs never get direct access to the hardware. The kernel checks permissions on every request. Even the root user, the admin account that can do almost anything, runs in user space and still has to ask the kernel.

Walls for trust

Two spaces also help a machine manage multiple accounts. The kernel keeps track of which user owns what, so one person can’t read or overwrite another person’s private data, while users can still share resources to keep the overall load down. This is mainly a product of its time: computers used to be so expensive that people split up their time on them, called time-sharing. The machine had to manage many user profiles without corrupting or leaking anyone’s data.

Walls that hide complexity

You don’t need to know how bits travel from memory to the CPU. You just need to know that clicking a button pulls up your web browser. Everything comes down to abstractions. Engineers love to hide the details the end user doesn’t need to see. The user just needs to know which inputs produce the outputs they want.

Look at the first computers compared to now. We kept adding abstractions. Operating systems arrived to manage programs and processes as they grew with time and Moore’s law. A program is many abstractions in one: it’s built on system calls and other Unix commands. A web browser is a document viewer and a network client in one.

Why it matters

At the end of the day, these systems are set up to get as many people using computers as possible. Nobody wants to set up every piece of their computer like IKEA furniture. And remember: when these systems were first designed, they were still using time-sharing. Not everyone had a computer like we do today.

item.title: Iteration
item.description:
There I was. It was a hot summer going into a breathtaking fall. I wanted to go grab a pumpkin from the grocery store and decorate it. So I put on my shoes, walked out the door, and made sure I had my phone and necklace. I never leave without them anymore. You may ask why? Am I that popular?

The truth is, I was doing some homebrewing at my house. It’s 2026, so of course I have AI doing all the heavy lifting, and I’m just here to verify the overall structure. But I was developing this AI necklace that’s like an AI companion. But this is where stuff gets weird. The AI put something on my phone and the necklace. I tried to review the code, but I can’t even read it. It looks like it’s some sorta app, called “Hocus Pocus”. I opened it. It already had a dashboard open. I think, “But this is my first time opening it.” I let that thought drift as I was more intrigued, more interested in exploring what this is. It looks like it’s an MMORPG but for real life. Those stats are for anything you can think of. Then I see a stat maxed out at “100/100 imagination.” I thought that was weird, as I didn’t think I was any more or less imaginative than any other person.

I closed the app as I was walking down the steps to leave. I live on “Main Street”. So I’m really close to everything, including the grocery store. As I’m making my way down the street. I see some of my favorite people. Itdo the shopkeeper that could make you laugh on your worst days. Then Mrs. Johnson in the shop right next to his. She owned the local gaming cafe where I ended up every day after school. I pretty much grew up there. I know, without her, I wouldn’t be as into homebrewing as I am today.

But right as I’m waving to her, I see my buddy Jack running for me. Then, when he gets close, he yells into his phone, “water blast,” and out of thin air, an impossible blast of water shoots out of his phone. I’m instantly shocked and dripping wet. But he drops his phone, and the water stops. I ask him what the hell that was for. He is just laughing, rolling on the ground. As he does, I try to understand what just happened. I say out loud, “HOW DID YOU DO THAT? THAT’S AN IMPOSSIBLE AMOUNT OF WATER!” Jack is still trying to catch your breath from laughing. He finally gets up. “You’re on the app, right?” I ask, “What the hell are you talking about?” He looks down and says, “Oh, I thought I saw you on an app I have, but I’m not allowed to talk about it, unless you’re also on the app.” I ask, “What’s it called?” he replies, “I can’t say; it just automatically downloads to random phones.

No one knows how many people are on it. But estimates are around 3000 people. He pulls out his phone. Then shows me on a weird 3D-ish map. That’s how he knew I downloaded it. I pull out my phone to see, and he’s on my map too. I zoom out of the map. Then I ask, “Why can’t I see everyone?” He replies, “It’s a distance parameter. You have to be ‘x’ feet away before people show up.” I’ve only ever seen 3 others, not including you. But I was scared, so I ran as far as I could. But today I saw the map populate, then I saw you, so I took my shot ,hoping it was you.

I began clicking through all the options. Then, when I saw Duel, I clicked on Jack on the map. I asked if he’d ever done it. He said, “No, want to?” I replied, “Of course”. I clicked Duel, and it put us in a match. Everything around us changes to this chromatic representation of the real world. Jack and I were pushed 50 feet apart. I yelled, “What’s going on?” He replied, “I know just as much as you now.”

An echoing voice bounced off the wall, saying, “You may use any magic in this match, and to BEGIN!” Jack didn’t waste any time; he hit me with another water blast. This time it felt stronger. It was hard to keep my feet planted. While I was holding my breath. As the water stopped dripping off me, I yelled, “How do I know what magic I have?” Jack replied, “It’s the bookshelf tab, then spells.” Of course, I go straight for the table of contents, looking for a crazy spell. Found it, I said. I begin to yell, “Fearsome, - “, Jack cuts me off. “HAHAHA, you can’t cast that. Look, it says right here this is a legendary spell. You would need to be at least max level, and even then I think it’s still a myth.” I say fuck it, “FEARSOME, THE ANCIENT DRAGON” Out of nowhere, a highly polite 19th-century British man shows up in the middle of us. Jack just starts laughing because he’s literally in back and white. He slowly opens his briefcase, and the red-yellowish glow is emerging and engulfing the chromium environment. As it gets brighter, it gets so blinding I close my eyes. Even with my eyes closed, I see red like a picture in my head. Then the jets of wind are swirling all the air around, causing so much turbulence that I can barely stay on my feet. I feel a hand grab me to keep me from falling. I think, “That must be Jack.” Then, just as fast as it happened, it stopped, and I opened my eyes, and it was black. I couldn’t see anything. All I could see was that it wasn’t Jack holding me up; it was the man.
